description: We are on a mission, and we are going to tell you nothing about it at present, That's all we can say! 😎
summary:
We developed CrewCheck, an intuitive web application designed to monitor astronaut health during long-duration space missions. Addressing the challenge of limited medical access in space, CrewCheck allows astronauts to log four critical daily metrics: sleep hours, mood, exercise duration, and heart rate. Built with React and Vite, the app utilizes local storage to track these metrics and features dynamic visual graphs to monitor health trends over time.

Crucially, CrewCheck maps these daily logs directly to NASA’s Human Research Program (HRP) hazards; such as tracking exercise to mitigate bone loss, and sleep/mood to monitor isolation risks. The application features a rule-based warning engine that scans recent data and triggers visual alerts on the dashboard if thresholds are breached (e.g., low sleep for three consecutive days).

This project is important because it acts as an early-warning system for astronauts who are months away from a doctor. By empowering crew members with real-time, automated health insights, CrewCheck helps prevent physical and psychological decline, ensuring the crew remains mission-ready and safe.
details:
What does it do or how does it work?
CrewCheck is a web dashboard where astronauts log five daily metrics (sleep, mood, exercise, heart rate, radiation dose). The app saves this data locally, generates dynamic trend graphs, and uses a rule-based engine to trigger visual warning cards if health thresholds are breached over consecutive days.

What benefits does it have?
It automates health surveillance where no immediate medical help exists. By converting raw daily data into automated alerts, it prevents minor physical or psychological issues from escalating into severe, mission-threatening conditions.

What is the intended impact of the project?
To safeguard astronaut health during long-duration missions (like Mars). Early detection of decline ensures the crew remains physically and mentally resilient enough to complete mission objectives safely.

What tools, coding languages, hardware, or software did you use?
Frontend: React.js, Vite, JavaScript, HTML5/CSS3. Graphs: Chart.js. Data: localStorage (client-side). Version Control: GitHub/Codespaces. Deployment: Vercel. No specialized hardware was used.

How is your project creative?
Instead of being a standard fitness tracker, it explicitly maps daily metrics to severe NASA hazards (e.g., low exercise = bone loss risk). The engine also uses a consecutive-day logic algorithm, mimicking real medical trend analysis rather than reacting to a single bad day.

What factors did your team consider?
We factored in the 39-hour hackathon limit and team experience by prioritizing a robust MVP over complex backends. We also designed a dark, high-contrast UI to reduce eye strain in space and used client-side storage to account for potential internet unreliability.

How does it align with NASA's Human Research Program (HRP) hazards?
The app directly maps five metrics to HRP risks: Sleep and Mood to Behavioral Health & Isolation; Exercise to Bone/Muscle Loss; Heart Rate to Gravity Fields; Radiation Dose to Space Radiation; and Logging Consistency to Distance from Earth.

What is the future scalability plan for actual spacecraft?
While this prototype uses localStorage, a production version would use an offline-first database to securely sync with mission control, allowing Earth-based flight surgeons to receive real-time automated alerts.
